segments.title: A practical guide to medieval life
segments.summary: Toni Mount's guide surveys medieval English society through practical questions about housing, food, work, family life, law, and warfare.
segments.body: The book uses the practical questions a person would face in medieval England as its organizing principle. Its chapters cover class and housing, belief, clothing, food, health, work, leisure, family, warfare, and law. Questions about women's work, children's education, policing, courts, military service, veterans, and survival turn those broad themes into a guide to everyday choices and constraints. Warfare sits among the social institutions that supported or limited it, giving viewers a sense of the book's breadth before the reading from its chapter on pets.

evidence.note: The review lists the book's practical chapters, including its section on warfare.

segments.title: Animals as household workers and companions
segments.summary: Livestock and working animals shared space with medieval households, while pets offered companionship, warmth, and displays of status.
segments.body: A poorer family might share its home with a cow, goat, or chickens, gaining winter warmth while keeping the animals safe at night. Horses and oxen supplied traction, dogs guarded property and herded sheep, and cats protected stored grain from vermin. Animals also supplied food, clothing, and transport, while a knight's warhorse made rank visible. Companion animals included squirrels, birds, spiders, monkeys, and parrots as well as cats and small dogs. An ermine or stoat in a da Vinci portrait provides another example of an animal used to signal the sitter's social position.

evidence.note: The passage contrasts livestock and working animals with companion animals.

segments.title: Cats between pest control and suspicion
segments.summary: Cats appear as useful mousers and affordable fur, but also as animals burdened by moral suspicion and religious imagery.
segments.body: Cats had a contradictory place in medieval life. They killed rats and mice, and the sumptuary laws of 1363 allowed lower-status people to wear cat fur for warmth. Edward, Duke of York's hunting treatise nevertheless described cats as devilish because they tormented prey before killing it. Practical acceptance appears at Exeter Cathedral, which paid its cats one penny a week and gave them a small opening through the north transept wall so they could hunt vermin. A guide for enclosed women allowed cats as companions while warning that affection for them must not outrank love of God. Records of purchases and a lawsuit show that cats were valued property, while a manuscript illumination depicts them hunting rodents and birds, roaming at night, and sleeping beside the fire.

evidence.note: The review discusses cats' vermin-control role, fur, religious associations, and documentary examples.

segments.title: Dogs, work, loyalty, and medieval medicine
segments.summary: A discussion of dogs links practical tracking and guarding duties with stories of loyalty and striking medieval medical beliefs.
segments.body: Dogs worked as trackers, sheep guards, and defenders of their owners' property. The medieval bestiary discussed here gives dogs six pages while granting cats only a brief mention. Classical stories praise dogs that refuse to leave dead or dying masters, but Richard II's dog Mathe reportedly transferred its allegiance to Henry IV after the king's deposition. Henry treated the change as a good omen for his reign and for England's loyalty to the new regime, though a joke about steak in his pocket undercuts the political symbolism. The passage then turns to unsettling medieval remedies, including claims that a dog's tongue could heal intestinal wounds and that boiled puppies could treat gout.

evidence.note: The review covers dogs' working duties, classical loyalty tales, Richard II's dog, and medical remedies.

segments.title: Lap dogs as status and memorial companions
segments.summary: The review uses lap dogs in tombs and memorial brasses to show how pets could signal status, comfort, and enduring affection.
segments.body: Small dogs were companions and status symbols for elite women. In cold, draughty buildings they could also warm an owner's hands or feet like a living hot-water bottle. Tomb sculpture and memorial brasses turn those private relationships into public evidence: dogs appear at women's feet in examples from Sussex and Derbyshire. Clerics, dukes, and knights were also commemorated with favored dogs. Comparable monuments in France and Flanders place the English examples within a wider aristocratic culture of companionship, status, and remembrance.

evidence.note: The passage describes lap dogs, tombs and brasses, and similar memorial customs beyond England.

segments.title: Why Toni Mount's book earns a recommendation
segments.summary: The review recommends Toni Mount's lively medieval-history guide and notes a small gender error in its copyright statement.
segments.body: The final verdict is enthusiastic: the book is fun to read, worthwhile, and strong enough to prompt an interest in more of Toni Mount's work. The review also sketches Mount's background in historical nonfiction, teaching, medieval medicine, costume interpretation, online courses, and medieval mystery novels. Her experience fits the book's combination of practical detail and an accessible format. The only criticism concerns a gender error in the copyright declaration, where Mount is identified with a male pronoun. The episode closes without adding a second review because each book deserves its own time.

evidence.note: The review evaluates the book, summarizes the author's background, and identifies the minor copyright-statement error.
